answer: The paper's ITL formula ITL = α/(1 − λW) holds quantitatively in BLIS at low arrival rates (5–20 req/s, MAPE < 0.1%) but breaks down structurally at higher rates. The breakdown is caused by a shape mismatch: BLIS's trained-physics latency model produces concave (decelerating) ITL growth with rate due to sub-linear MoE expert scaling and KV-bandwidth nonlinearities in StepTime(), while the formula predicts convex (accelerating) growth. A linear fit (R² > 0.975) outperforms the best-fit 1/(1−ρ) formula (R² = 0.919 AL, 0.947 AD) across rates 5–150 req/s. The formula overpredicts by 108% (AL) and 50% (AD) at rate=150. Removing finite-horizon transients (Q2–Q3 quartile restriction) worsens the fit, proving the breakdown is structural, not transient. Directional predictions hold: Always-Disaggregate (AD) delivers strictly lower ITL than Always-Local (AL) at all tested rates (gap 0.06–1.69 ms), while paying strictly higher TTFT (penalty 4.4–9.6 ms), with the tradeoff improving at higher loads. Calibrated formula parameters confirm w_AL > w_AD (0.00471 > 0.00369), consistent with the paper's prediction.
